sections.heading: Ujjayanta Palace
sections.content: is the royal house, which stands in the Capital city of Agartala. Built by Maharaja Radha Kishore Manikya during 1899-1901, this two storied royal house is beautifully carved and sculpted in Indo-Greek style. High domes, well laid out gardens and parks, fountains and tanks make it an impressive structure. The palace is set with huge Mughal style gardens, beautified by pools and gardens and tiled floors. Particularly notable are the magnificently tiled floors, the ceiling of the Chinese Room which was crafted by artisans brought from China, and the carved front doors. The two-storied palace has three large domes, the largest of which is 86 ft (26 m) high from the ground and which rests a top a four-storied central tower.

sections.heading: Tripura- Monument- Rock Cut Carving in Tripura
sections.content: Tripura has beautiful rock cut carvings and stone images at Unakoti, Debtamura and Pilak. Most of these carvings are huge in size and made on vertical walls exposed in the open atmosphere.

sections.heading: Unakoti Palace
sections.content: Unakoti dating back to the eight or ninth century probably has the biggest bas-relief sculpture in India. The Legend- According to Hindu mythology, when Lord Shiva was proceeding to Kashi along with a crore of gods and goddesses he made a night halt at Unakoti. Shiva asked all the gods and goddesses to wake up before sun rise and proceed to Kashi. In the morning no one except Lord Shiva woke up, forcing him to set out for Kashi by himself and cursing the others to become stone images. Lord Shiva's curse fell upon them and as a result there are one less than a crore stone image carvings at Unakoti. The images found at Unakoti are of two types namely rock-carved figures and stone images. The most imposing sculpture is the immense 30 feet-high image of Lord Shiva called Unokotiswara Kal Bhairava carved in a vertical rock face. The colossal image in grey stone has an elaborate head. On each side of the central Shivas head-dress are two full size female figures - one of Goddess Durga standing on a lion and another female figure on the other side. In addition to this, three enormous images of Nandi the bull vahana of Lord Shiva are found half buried in the ground. A small, rock strewn stream flows near the central Shiva. Near the huge Shiva image, among scattered rocks, are the three imposing images of Lord Ganesha. There is a huge figure of the four - armed seated Ganesha and on its side two standing figures of Sarabhuja Ganesha with three tusks and the Asthabhuja Ganesha with four tusks- a rare sight to behold. Among the rock cut carvings, the central Shiva and gigantic Ganesha are certainly master pieces. There are various others stone as well as rock cut images at Unakoti.Every year a big fair popularly known as Ashokastami Mela is held here in the month of April which is visited by thousands of pilgrims.

sections.heading: Tripura- Monument- Palaces- Debatamura
sections.content: Debatamura is famous for its panels of rock carvings on the steep mountain wall on the bank of Gomati. There are huge images carved of Shiva, Vishnu, Kartika, Mahisasur Mardini, Durga and other gods and goddesses. This is also called Chabimura. These images dating back to fifteenth-sixteenth centuries are carved with a lot of dexterity on the rocky faces of Debtamura which is as steep as 90 degrees.

sections.heading: Tripura- Monument- Palaces- Pillak
sections.content: A treasure house of Hindu and Buddhist sculpture dating back to 8th and 9th centuries, Pillak boasts of beautiful images scattered in an area of about 10 Sq.Km. The terracotta plaques, stone images and seals found here reflect the existence of both Hinduism and Buddhism. Colossal stone images of Avalokiteshwar and Narasimha have also been found here. Communities of Tripura The Tripuris represent more than 50% of the total tribal population of the State. The Tripuris live on the slopes of hills in a group of five to fifty families. Tripuri women wear a skirt, called Pachra, which reaches down just below the knee. They weave in their loin-loom a small piece of cloth, which they call Risha, and they use this small piece of cloth as their top garment. sections.heading: Tripura Dance
sections.content: The culture of dance in Tripura is vibrant and associated with the ethnic tribes that are both indigenous and native. The Tripuri, the Reang, the Chakma, Halam (Malsum), and the Lushai community and Garo tribes are some of the groups that have exotic dress code and dance forms. The main folk dances are Hozagiri dance of Reang, Garia, Jhum, Maimita, Masak Sumani and Lebang boomani dances of Tripuri, Bizu dance of Chakma, Cheraw and welcome dances of Lusai, Hai-Hak dance of Malsum, Wangala dance of Garo, Sangraiaka, Chimithang, Padisha and abhangma dances of Mog Garia dances of Kalai and Jamatia, Gajan, Dhamail, Sari and Rabindra dances of Bengali and Basanta Rash and Pung chalam dances of Manipuri community. Each of them have their own traditional musical instruments. The important musical instruments are Khamb( Drum), Bamboo flute, Lebang, Sarinda, Do- Tara, and Khengrong, etc.

sections.heading: Tripura - Handicrafts - Cane and Bamboo Work
sections.content: Tripura is famous for its cane and bamboo handicrafts. They include table mats, floor mats, room dividers, decorated wall panels, and attractive furniture of cane. The Tripura mudah is a low stool made of bamboo and split cane. Bamboo is used in the body and rim structure; while split-cane is used in binding all elements and in the seat weave. Very intricate and exquisite bamboo and cane ornaments are also produced in Tripura. In Agartala, a few craftsmen prepare small woven animal forms from fine splints of bamboo. They are intended both as toys and as decorations. The forms are evolved by either weaving or braiding uniformally fine splints.

sections.heading: Tripura- Handicrafts- Basketry
sections.content: Basketry is an important craft of Tripura. The different types of baskets produced in the state include jamatia- firewood basket, riang- carrying basket, tukri, karawala tukri, laii, sempa khari-date basket, turi- grain storage basket, dulla and sudha - the traditional fish trap.

sections.heading: Tripura- Handicrafts- Pathla Rain Shield
sections.content: The Pathla from Tripura is a rain shield. The top cone has a base of 230 mm with a height of 110 mm, and the circular shade that is angled slightly downwards, has a diameter of 550 mm. A pentagon made up of five elements, each of which has three strips of bamboo, encircles the apex of the cone. The subsequent hexagons on the cone are also made with three strips to each element. Five wide interlocking strips of bamboo strengthen the apex of the cone. These strips are held in place by introducing them into the weave on the cone.

sections.heading: Tripura- Handicrafts- Handlooms
sections.content: The people of Tripura look to weaving as an inseparable part of life as it is the oldest industry in Tripura. Passed on from generation to generation the people of the state produce their own clothes with elegant designs and lasting texture using unique color combinations. Risa and Riha are two traditional handloom items of the state that are used during rituals. In Tripura, for a prospective birde, good knowledge of the craft of weaving is essential.

sections.heading: Tripura Government Museum
sections.content: The Tripura Government Museum is a treasure house of artifacts and manuscripts that are a feature of the rich history of the northeast. A store house of priceless pieces the museum is endowed with four galleries, namely the Archaeological gallery, Tribal Culture gallery Painting gallery and the Indian Sculpture gallery. The galleries showcase a wonderful collection of over 1645 historical artifacts. Scholars and historians can seek numismatic evidence through the numerous gold, silver and copper coins that the archaeological excavations have unraveled. Numerous pottery pieces, sculptures and terracotta, bronze figurines and primordial copper inscriptions have also been unearthed. Magnificent canvas oil paintings, sketches and illustrations, textiles as well as jewellery and ornaments also find pride of place in the museum's sprawling galleries. The museum is also endowed with a library that contains an enviable collection of rare and out print editions on the history, archeology, architecture and anthropology of Tripura.
